article.headline: China's Kunlun Opens a Video-Generation Rival to Runway and Kling
article.lede: A Chinese AI lab has open-sourced what it describes as the world's first 'infinite-length' video generation model, putting capabilities previously confined to subscription services nominally within reach of the public. The model, SkyReels V2, comes from SkyworkAI, the research arm of Kunlun Tech (300418.SZ) — a Shenzhen-listed game and technology company better known for social platforms across Southeast Asia and Africa than for frontier AI research. The actual story is more nuanced than the promotional framing suggests.
article.body:
SkyReels V2 is built around a technique called **Diffusion Forcing**, which allows the model to generate video in rolling segments rather than as a fixed-length clip. Conventional diffusion models apply a single noise schedule across all frames simultaneously, which caps output at whatever duration the model was trained on. Diffusion Forcing assigns independent noise levels to individual frame patches — *tokens*, in the jargon — using a non-decreasing schedule that lets the model treat the final seventeen frames of any completed segment as the starting point for the next, making the chain theoretically extendable without limit. The team's paper (arXiv 2504.13074) claims this reduces the combinatorial search space from roughly 10^48 to 10^32 possible states, which is the mathematical justification for calling indefinite generation feasible.

The family ships in two parameter sizes — 1.3 billion and 14 billion — at resolutions of 540p and 720p. On VBench, an academic benchmark developed at Nanyang Technological University, the flagship 14B model scores 83.9 percent overall, edging past competing open-weight model WanVideo 2.1 at 83.7 percent and HunyuanVideo, a rival open model from Tencent Holdings (700.HK), at 82.7 percent. In the team's own human-evaluation study — a 1,020-prompt instrument the researchers designed and administered themselves — V2 outperforms Kling 1.6, the model from Kuaishou Technology (1024.HK), and Runway's Gen3 on average text-to-video quality. On image-to-video tasks, however, the commercial models fight back: Runway's Gen4 and Kling 1.6 Pro both outperform V2 on motion quality in the same exercise.

The tweet's claim that users can create 'unlimited high-quality videos without paying' deserves scrutiny on two fronts. The 1.3B model at 540p requires roughly 14.7 gigabytes of GPU memory in its most frugal configuration; the 14B flagship at 720p demands around 51 gigabytes — an A100-class multi-GPU setup that most individuals do not own, and which cloud providers rent at rates that quickly exceed a Runway or Kling subscription for typical usage. 'Infinite' also describes an architectural property rather than a reliable practical output: the *autoregressive* segment-chaining approach accumulates small inconsistencies over time, and the team acknowledges that **scene drift** — a gradual incoherence in subject appearance and background detail — becomes measurable beyond roughly thirty to sixty seconds. Genuine hour-long generation without perceptible degradation, the paper concedes, 'is still an active area of research.'

The model's license adds a further wrinkle. The Skywork Community License permits commercial use but is not a standard open-source instrument such as Apache 2.0 or MIT. Its binding terms live in a separate PDF rather than inline in the repository, and the agreement includes language — reflecting Chinese regulatory requirements — that organizations deploying the model for internet services may face registration obligations. None of this makes V2 unusable commercially, but enterprises should read the full agreement rather than treat 'open-source' as equivalent to 'unrestricted.'

Two genuine technical contributions distinguish V2 from prior open-weight video models. The first is a *motion reinforcement learning* pipeline: the team trained a reward model on human-annotated preference pairs — clean footage versus synthetically distorted motion — and applied a form of *direct preference optimization* to improve physical plausibility in generated footage. Motion realism has been the persistent weakness of open-source video generation relative to commercial products, and V2's human-evaluation scores suggest the RL step meaningfully narrows that gap. The second is SkyCaptioner-V1, an open-sourced video-understanding model the team claims outperforms existing video captioners — a tool aimed at practitioners building automated labeling pipelines for training their own models.

concepts.definition: A video generation technique that assigns independent noise levels to each frame patch (token) rather than applying a single global noise schedule across all frames. By using a non-decreasing schedule, the model can generate video in rolling segments, each conditioned on the tail of the previous — enabling arbitrarily long output without a hard frame cap.

A class of generative AI model that learns to produce data — images, video, audio — by learning to reverse a gradual noising process. During generation, the model starts from random noise and iteratively denoises toward a coherent output. Most modern AI image and video generators use this approach.

The basic units a video generation model processes. In vision models, a token typically corresponds to a small rectangular patch of pixels in a single frame rather than a word. A video is broken into a large grid of such patches across all its frames; the model learns relationships between them to produce coherent motion.

A generation strategy in which a model produces output sequentially, with each new segment conditioned on what came before. In video, this means generating a short clip, then treating its final frames as context to generate the next clip, and so on. The approach enables indefinite extension but accumulates small errors over time.

An academic benchmark developed at Nanyang Technological University (NTU) for evaluating text-to-video generation models across dimensions including visual quality, prompt adherence, and temporal consistency. It is one of the few independent, standardized evaluation frameworks in the field.

A failure mode in long-form AI video generation where subtle inconsistencies — changes in a subject's appearance, shifts in background detail, gradual loss of stylistic coherence — accumulate across segments over time. It is the primary practical limit on so-called 'infinite-length' video generation.

A reinforcement-learning technique for aligning AI model outputs with human preferences. Instead of training a separate reward model and using it to update the main model via complex RL loops, DPO directly optimizes the model's policy on human-labeled preference pairs — for example, 'this clip of motion is better than that distorted one.'

An AI model whose trained parameters (weights) are publicly released for download and local use, as distinct from a fully 'open-source' model, which additionally requires the training code, data, and pipeline to be public. Open-weight models can be run locally and fine-tuned, but typically carry custom license restrictions on commercial use.

A training technique applied after a model's initial pre-training phase, using human-annotated preference data about motion quality to steer the model toward physically plausible, artifact-free movement. In SkyReels V2's case, this involved pairing clean video with synthetically distorted versions and training a reward model to distinguish them.

repos.summary: The official repository for SkyReels V2, containing inference code, model download links, and documentation for all task variants: Text-to-Video, Image-to-Video, Diffusion Forcing (infinite-length), and Camera Director. Includes CLI usage examples, per-configuration VRAM tables, multi-GPU acceleration setup via xDiT, and the full benchmark tables from the paper. Also bundles SkyCaptioner-V1, an open-sourced video-understanding and captioning model.

article.fact_check: The tweet's claim that users can create 'unlimited high-quality videos without paying' is misleading on both counts. Running the 14B flagship model at 720p requires approximately 51 gigabytes of GPU memory — an enterprise-grade multi-GPU configuration — making cloud compute costs likely to exceed a conventional subscription for typical usage volumes. The 1.3B model is more accessible (roughly 15GB VRAM) but produces lower-quality output. 'Unlimited' refers to an architectural property of the Diffusion Forcing approach; in practice, the team's own paper acknowledges that scene coherence degrades measurably beyond thirty to sixty seconds, and that long-form generation without drift 'is still an active area of research.' The model's comparative benchmarks also rely partly on SkyReels-Bench, an evaluation instrument designed and administered by the same team.

ticker_300418-sz.blurb: Kunlun Tech Co., Ltd. provides internet value-added services in China and internationally, including short drama and AI short drama platforms, AI music, AI games, AI social networking products, and browser advertising. The company also engages in artificial intelligence technology development, music social platforms, online game operation, and investment management. Formerly known as Beijing Kunlun Tech Co., Ltd., it changed its name in June 2021 and is headquartered in Beijing.
